en.title: Artificial Intelligence: the whole course
en.short: What AI covers, how AI degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the study of agents that perceive their environment and act to achieve goals. An agent may be a program, a robot or a system that recommends decisions. AI covers search, reasoning, knowledge representation, planning, learning, perception, language and robotics. It is not only machine learning, and machine learning is not only deep learning. The field also asks what intelligence is, what can be computed, and how to build systems that are useful, safe and fair. It draws on computer science, mathematics, logic, probability, economics and psychology. The aim of a degree is to give you the principles and the practical skill to build and evaluate such systems.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Degrees differ by country and institution. A first degree in AI may be a BSc in Artificial Intelligence, a BSc in Computer Science with AI options, or a related engineering degree. Length and awards vary. In Nigeria, many BSc programmes run for four years, and the National Universities Commission (NUC) sets minimum standards through its Core Curriculum and Minimum Academic Standards (CCMAS); AI may appear as a course or an option within computing, and some universities offer dedicated programmes. Check your department handbook for the current rules. In England, a BSc usually takes three years and a taught master’s one year. In South Africa, a three-year BSc is often followed by an Honours year. Polytechnics and colleges may award diplomas with a stronger practical focus. A master’s degree usually adds advanced courses and a dissertation. Always confirm length, accreditation and award with your own institution.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually moves from foundations to core AI and then to advanced study. The intro stage builds tools: Python programming for AI; discrete mathematics for AI; linear algebra for AI; probability and statistics for AI; calculus and optimisation for AI; logic and formal reasoning; algorithms and complexity for AI; data literacy and preprocessing; and foundations of intelligent agents. These give you the language for later work. For example, linear algebra describes vectors and matrices, probability describes uncertainty, and optimisation finds the best value of a function.

The core stage covers classical AI and machine learning. It begins with uninformed search, informed search and heuristics (rules of thumb that guide search), adversarial search and games (search in competitive settings), and constraint satisfaction problems (problems defined by variables and limits on their values). It continues with knowledge representation and ontologies (structured vocabularies of concepts and relations), propositional logic and inference, first-order logic and inference, and classical planning (finding sequences of actions). It then treats uncertainty and probabilistic reasoning, Bayesian networks (graphs of probabilistic dependencies), machine learning fundamentals, neural networks and deep learning basics (layered models inspired by neurons), natural language processing, computer vision, robotics and embodied AI, reinforcement learning (learning from rewards), and AI ethics and governance.

The master’s stage deepens the subject: advanced machine learning, deep learning architectures, probabilistic graphical models, and research methods in AI. The exact order and optional courses vary, so use your handbook.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text: Study by building. Write Python every week and implement small versions of search, logic and learning algorithms. Trace algorithms by hand on tiny examples before running code. For mathematics, practise problems until definitions and proofs feel natural. Work with real datasets, but split training and test data correctly and report honest results. Read one paper or documentation page at a time and summarise it in your own words. Keep a project notebook. Use AI tools only under your university’s rules, and be able to explain every line you submit. Revise ethics and governance alongside technical work, not after it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text: Common mistakes include treating AI as only machine learning, or machine learning as only deep learning. Students confuse search strategies, forget the difference between a heuristic and an exact method, and use a library without understanding its assumptions. In data work, they leak test information into training, overfit small samples, or report accuracy on unbalanced data without other measures. In logic and probability, they skip definitions and then misapply rules. They also anthropomorphise systems, ignore bias and privacy, and leave projects and reports late. Check regulations and deadlines early, and test edge cases.

keyPoints: AI is the study of agents that perceive and act, not only machine learning.
Foundations in programming, mathematics, logic and data come before core AI.
Core AI includes search, knowledge representation, reasoning, planning, learning, perception and ethics.
Master’s study adds advanced machine learning, deep architectures, graphical models and research methods.
Study by implementing algorithms, tracing them by hand and working with real data honestly.
Check your own handbook for degree length, awards and regulations, because these differ by country and institution.

en.title: Python programming for AI
en.short: Python basics for AI: variables, control flow, functions, modules, NumPy, pandas, notebooks, testing and debugging.

sections.heading: Variables and control flow
sections.text:
A variable is a name bound to a Python object. Common types are int, float, str and bool. Python is dynamically typed: a name can later refer to a different type. Control flow decides which lines run. if, elif and else choose a branch. for repeats over a sequence; while repeats while a condition holds. Indentation marks a block.

Example:
total = 0
for x in [2, 4, 6]:
    total = total + x
The loop adds 2, 4, 6; total is 12.

sections.heading: Functions and modules
sections.text: A function packages code under a name. def mean(values): return sum(values) / len(values) defines one. Calling mean([2, 4, 6]) returns 4.0 because 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Parameters are names in the definition; arguments are values passed in. A module is a file of Python code imported with import. The standard library is a collection of modules; packages such as NumPy are imported the same way. Keep functions small and clearly named.

sections.heading: NumPy arrays and pandas data frames
sections.text: A NumPy array is a grid of values, usually all the same type. It supports vectorised arithmetic: an operation applies to every element without an explicit loop. For example, a = np.array([2, 4, 6]); a * 2 gives array([4, 8, 12]) and a.mean() gives 4.0. A pandas DataFrame is a table with labelled columns and rows. df = pd.DataFrame({'x': [1, 2], 'y': [3, 4]}) makes a two-column table; df['x'].sum() is 3.

sections.heading: Notebooks, testing and debugging
sections.text: A notebook such as Jupyter is an interactive document of cells. Code cells run in a kernel and keep state, so run cells in order. A test checks that code gives the expected result. Use assert mean([2, 4, 6]) == 4.0, or a framework such as unittest or pytest. Debugging means finding and fixing errors in code. Read the traceback bottom up, print intermediate values, or set a breakpoint. For a small AI exercise, test shapes and known cases before trusting output.

keyPoints: A variable names a Python object; control flow uses if, for and while with indentation.
Functions take parameters and return values; modules let you reuse code with import.
NumPy arrays support vectorised arithmetic; pandas DataFrames hold labelled tabular data.
Run notebook cells in order because the kernel keeps state.
Test small functions with assert or pytest on known inputs.
Debug by reading the traceback, printing values, or using a breakpoint.

en.title: Discrete mathematics for AI
en.short: Sets, relations, functions, graphs, trees, counting and proof techniques for AI.

sections.heading: Sets and functions
sections.text: A set is a collection of distinct objects. The union A ∪ B contains elements in A or B; the intersection A ∩ B contains elements in both. |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. A function f: A → B assigns one element of B to each element of A. A is the domain, B the codomain, and the range is the values produced. In AI, a classifier is a function from inputs to labels.

sections.heading: Relations and graphs
sections.text: A relation on A is a subset of A × A; it may be reflexive, symmetric or transitive. An equivalence relation has all three and splits A into disjoint classes. A graph G = (V, E) has vertices V and edges E. A path is a sequence of adjacent vertices. A graph can model a state space: vertices are states and edges are moves. A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. A rooted tree has a root and parent-child links. Search trees are common in AI.

sections.heading: Combinatorics
sections.text: Combinatorics counts arrangements. n distinct items can be ordered in n! ways. A k-element subset of n items can be chosen in C(n, k) = n! ÷ (k!(n − k)!) ways. The product rule: m options and n options give m × n pairs. Example: a Boolean feature vector of length 4 has 2⁴ = 16 possible vectors. If exactly 2 features are true, there are C(4, 2) = 4! ÷ (2!2!) = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 such vectors. Brute-force search over all assignments grows quickly.

sections.heading: Proof techniques
sections.text: Direct proof starts from definitions and reaches the claim. Proof by contradiction assumes the claim is false and derives an impossibility. Proof by contrapositive proves that if the claim is false then the premise is false. Mathematical induction proves a base case and an induction step. One counterexample disproves a universal claim. In AI, proofs show termination, invariants or universal properties.

keyPoints: A set is a collection of distinct objects; |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.
A function maps each input to exactly one output, and a classifier is one example.
A relation is a set of ordered pairs; an equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
A graph has vertices and edges; a tree is a connected graph with no cycles.
n items can be ordered in n! ways, and k items can be chosen from n in C(n, k) = n! ÷ (k!(n − k)!) ways.
Proof by induction needs a base case and an induction step; one counterexample disproves a universal claim.

en.title: Linear algebra for AI
en.short: Vectors, matrices, rank, eigenvalues and SVD, and how they represent data and transformations.

sections.heading: Vectors and matrices
sections.text:
A vector is an ordered list of numbers, written as a column. In AI, a data point such as an image or a word embedding is often a vector in Rⁿ. A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers; an m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. A dataset with N examples and d features is an N × d matrix.

Matrix operations: add matrices of the same shape entry by entry; multiply by a scalar; multiply A (m × n) by B (n × p) to get C (m × p), where cᵢⱼ = Σₖ aᵢₖ bₖⱼ. The transpose Aᵀ swaps rows and columns.

sections.heading: Rank and transformations
sections.text:
Rank is the number of linearly independent rows (or columns) of a matrix: rows that cannot be built from the others. It measures how much independent information the matrix carries. A square matrix is invertible only if its rank equals its size.

Matrix multiplication represents a linear transformation: y = Ax maps vector x to y. A 2 × 2 matrix can rotate or scale points in the plane. The columns of A are the images of the basis vectors.

sections.heading: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
sections.text:
An eigenvector v of a square matrix A is a nonzero vector that A only scales: Av = λv. The scalar λ is the eigenvalue. They describe directions that a transformation leaves unchanged.

For A = [[2,1],[1,2]], take v = [1,1]ᵀ.
Av = [3,3]ᵀ = 3v, so λ = 3.
Also v = [1,−1]ᵀ gives Av = [1,−1]ᵀ = 1v, so λ = 1.

sections.heading: Singular value decomposition
sections.text:
Singular value decomposition writes any m × n matrix A as A = UΣVᵀ. U and V are orthogonal matrices: their columns are unit vectors at right angles. Σ is diagonal with non-negative singular values, which measure how much A stretches each direction. The number of nonzero singular values equals the rank.

SVD is used to compress data and for principal component analysis (PCA), a dimensionality reduction method. Keeping only the largest singular values gives a low-rank approximation of A.

keyPoints: A vector is an ordered list of numbers; a matrix is a rectangular array.
For A (m × n) and B (n × p), the product C = AB has cᵢⱼ = Σₖ aᵢₖ bₖⱼ.
Rank is the number of linearly independent rows or columns; a square matrix is invertible only if rank equals size.
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors satisfy Av = λv for a square matrix A.
SVD writes A = UΣVᵀ with non-negative singular values; their count equals the rank.
SVD supports data compression and PCA.

en.title: Probability and statistics for AI
en.short: Random variables, distributions, expectation, Bayes’ rule, sampling, estimation and hypothesis testing for AI.

sections.heading: Random variables
sections.text: A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. Discrete variables take countable values; continuous variables take any value in a range. Common distributions in AI: Bernoulli for yes/no, categorical for class labels, binomial for counts of successes, Gaussian (normal) for continuous measurements and noise. The probability mass function gives P(X = x) for discrete variables; the probability density function gives density for continuous ones.

sections.heading: Expectation and variance
sections.text: Expectation is the long-run average: E[X] = Σ x P(x) for discrete X. Variance measures spread: Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − μ², where μ = E[X]. Standard deviation is √Var(X).

sections.heading: Conditional probability and Bayes
sections.text: Conditional probability is P(A|B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B), the chance of A given B. Bayes’ rule turns this around: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) ÷ P(B). Worked example: a spam filter. Prior P(spam) = 0.3. The word "free" appears in 80% of spam and 10% of ham (legitimate email). P(free|spam) = 0.8, P(free|ham) = 0.1. P(free) = 0.8 × 0.3 + 0.1 × 0.7 = 0.24 + 0.07 = 0.31. P(spam|free) = 0.8 × 0.3 ÷ 0.31 = 0.24 ÷ 0.31 ≈ 0.774, about 77%.

sections.heading: Sampling and testing
sections.text: A sample is a subset of data. The sample mean estimates the population mean. Its standard error is σ ÷ √n, where σ is the population standard deviation and n is the sample size. Estimation gives a point estimate (a single value) or a confidence interval (a range). Hypothesis testing starts with a null hypothesis H0, often "no difference". A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming H0 is true. If p is below a chosen significance level α, reject H0. In AI evaluation, use these ideas to compare models on test data and to report uncertainty, not just a single accuracy score.

keyPoints: E[X] = Σ x P(x) for a discrete random variable.
Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².
Bayes’ rule: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) ÷ P(B).
The standard error of a sample mean is σ ÷ √n.
A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if H0 is true.
Common AI distributions include Bernoulli, categorical, binomial and Gaussian.

en.title: Calculus and optimisation for AI
en.short: Derivatives, gradients, chain rule, convexity, constraints and gradient descent, with worked calculations.

sections.heading: Derivatives
sections.text: A derivative measures how fast a function changes. For f(x), df/dx is the slope of the tangent at x. For example, d(3x² + 2x)/dx = 6x + 2. At x = 1 this derivative is 8, so f rises 8 times as fast as x there. A stationary point has df/dx = 0; it may be a minimum, maximum or neither.

sections.heading: Gradients and chain rule
sections.text:
A partial derivative differentiates with respect to one variable while holding the others fixed. For f(x,y) = x²y + y², partial f / partial x = 2xy and partial f / partial y = x² + 2y. At (2,1) the gradient is (4,6), which points in the direction of steepest increase.

The chain rule handles composed functions. If y = (3x + 1)², then dy/dx = 2(3x + 1) × 3 = 6(3x + 1).

sections.heading: Convexity and constraints
sections.text:
A function is convex if the line segment between any two points on its graph lies on or above the graph. For one variable, convexity means f''(x) ≥ 0. Any local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum.

Constrained optimisation minimises f subject to a constraint g = 0. Lagrange multipliers form L = f + λg and set its partial derivatives to zero. Example: minimise f = x² + y² subject to x + y = 1. L = x² + y² + λ(x + y − 1). Then 2x + λ = 0, 2y + λ = 0 and x + y = 1, so x = y = 0.5 and λ = −1.

sections.heading: Gradient descent
sections.text:
Gradient descent minimises a function by stepping against the gradient. The update is x_new = x_old − α df/dx, where α is the learning rate. For f(x) = x², df/dx = 2x. Start at x = 4 with α = 0.1:

x1 = 4 − 0.1 × 8 = 3.2
x2 = 3.2 − 0.1 × 6.4 = 2.56

These approach the minimum at x = 0. A large α can overshoot; a small α is slow.

keyPoints: Derivative df/dx gives the slope; stationary points have df/dx = 0.
Partial derivatives hold other variables fixed; the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives.
The chain rule multiplies derivatives: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.
A convex function has f''(x) ≥ 0, and any local minimum is a global minimum.
Lagrange multipliers solve equality constraints by setting partial derivatives of L = f + λg to zero.
Gradient descent updates x_new = x_old − α df/dx, where α is the learning rate.

en.title: Logic and formal reasoning
en.short: Propositional and predicate logic: syntax, truth tables, inference, soundness and translation.

sections.heading: Propositions and syntax
sections.text: Propositional logic treats statements as units. A proposition is true or false, such as P = 'Ada studies'. Connectives are ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (implies) and ↔ (if and only if). Syntax gives rules for well-formed formulas: a proposition letter is a formula; if A and B are formulas, so are ¬A, (A ∧ B), (A ∨ B), (A → B) and (A ↔ B). For example, P → Q is well formed.

sections.heading: Truth tables
sections.text:
Semantics assigns truth values. A truth table lists every combination and the compound value. For implication, P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false:
P Q | P → Q
T T | T
T F | F
F T | T
F F | T
A tautology is true in every row; a contradiction is false in every row; a formula is satisfiable if true in at least one row. Equivalent formulas have the same column.

sections.heading: Predicate logic
sections.text: Predicate logic, also called first-order logic, adds objects, properties and relations. A predicate such as Student(x) means 'x is a student'. Quantifiers are ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists). The domain fixes the objects. Translation needs care. 'Every student is kind' becomes ∀x (Student(x) → Kind(x)). 'Some student is kind' becomes ∃x (Student(x) ∧ Kind(x)). The first uses → because not every object is a student; the second uses ∧ because the object must satisfy both parts.

sections.heading: Inference and properties
sections.text: An inference rule takes premises and yields a conclusion. Modus ponens: from P and P → Q infer Q. Modus tollens: from ¬Q and P → Q infer ¬P. Example: 'If Ada studies, she passes. Ada studies. Therefore Ada passes.' A proof is a chain of steps. A proof system is sound if every provable conclusion is true whenever the premises are true. It is complete if every valid conclusion has a proof. Soundness blocks wrong conclusions; completeness says the rules are strong enough.

keyPoints: Propositional connectives are ¬, ∧, ∨, → and ↔; P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.
A tautology is true in every row; a contradiction is false in every row.
∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) translates 'all P are Q'; ∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) translates 'some P are Q'.
Modus ponens infers Q from P and P → Q; modus tollens infers ¬P from ¬Q and P → Q.
Soundness means provable conclusions are true whenever the premises are true; completeness means every valid conclusion is provable.
Fix the domain and predicates before translating a sentence into logic.

en.title: Algorithms and complexity for AI
en.short: Core data structures, asymptotic notation and the cost of search and inference in AI.

sections.heading: Data structures
sections.text:
A list stores items in order. In an array, reading by index is O(1), but searching is O(n) and inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n). A queue is first in, first out: enqueue adds to the back and dequeue removes from the front, both O(1) with a linked list or circular array. A stack is last in, first out: push and pop are O(1).

A priority queue returns the item with the highest priority. A binary heap implements it with peek O(1), and insert and extract O(log n). A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges. An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space; an adjacency matrix uses O(V²).

sections.heading: Asymptotic notation
sections.text: Asymptotic notation describes how cost grows with input size n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. Big O gives an upper bound: f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than g. Big Omega gives a lower bound: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f grows at least as fast as g. Big Theta gives a tight bound: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) means f grows at the same rate as g. For example, 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²) and also Θ(n²). The constants 3, 5 and 2 do not change the growth class.

sections.heading: Search and inference cost
sections.text: The complexity of a search or inference procedure is the number of basic steps it takes as a function of input size. Many AI problems are combinatorial: a procedure that examines every combination can take time exponential in the number of variables. For example, a procedure that checks 2^n states takes 2^20 = 1,048,576 steps when n = 20. When n = 30 it takes 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 steps, which is 1,024 times more. At one microsecond per step, that is about 1,074 seconds, or nearly 18 minutes. Polynomial-time procedures scale far better, so choosing the right data structure and algorithm matters.

keyPoints: A binary heap priority queue gives O(1) peek and O(log n) insert and extract.
An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space; an adjacency matrix uses O(V²).
Big O is an upper bound, big Omega a lower bound, and big Theta a tight bound.
3n² + 5n + 2 is Θ(n²).
A procedure that checks 2^n states takes 1,048,576 steps at n = 20 and 1,073,741,824 at n = 30.
Exponential growth makes exhaustive search and inference impractical for large problems.

en.title: Data literacy and preprocessing
en.short: Data types, cleaning, missing values, scaling, encoding, plots, splits and bias.

sections.heading: Data and sources
sections.text:
Data is recorded facts or measurements. Structured data sits in rows and columns; unstructured data includes text, images and audio. Variables are numerical (discrete counts or continuous measurements) or categorical (nominal labels with no order, such as city, or ordinal labels with order, such as small, medium, large).

Sources include surveys, sensors, logs, public datasets and the web. Record the source, unit and collection date, because these affect use.

sections.heading: Cleaning and missing values
sections.text:
Cleaning removes duplicates, fixes inconsistent formats and checks impossible values, such as an age of −5. Do not delete an outlier automatically; investigate it. For missing values, ask why they are missing. Options are deleting rows or columns, or imputing, which fills in the missing value with the mean, median or mode. Add a missing-value flag when the gap itself may carry information.

Example: ages 20, 25, missing, 30. The observed mean is 25, so mean imputation gives 25.

sections.heading: Scaling and encoding
sections.text:
Feature scaling puts numerical columns on comparable ranges. Min-max scaling maps x to (x − min) ÷ (max − min). Standardisation maps x to (x − mean) ÷ standard deviation. Example: scores 40, 60, 80. Mean = 60. Min-max gives 0, 0.5, 1. Standardisation gives −1.22, 0, 1.22, with standard deviation 16.33.

Categorical variables need encoding. One-hot encoding makes one binary column per category; label encoding gives each category an integer, which suits ordered categories but misleads for unordered ones.

sections.heading: Plots, splits and bias
sections.text:
Exploratory plots show shape and problems: histograms for one numerical variable, box plots for spread and outliers, scatter plots for two numerical variables, bar charts for category counts.

Before modelling, split data into training and test sets, for example 80 training and 20 test rows. Fit scaling and imputation on the training set only, then apply them to the test set, to avoid data leakage. For a 30/70 class split in 100 rows, a stratified 80/20 split, which preserves class proportions, keeps 24 and 56 in training. Bias enters through convenience samples, missing groups, faulty instruments and historical unfairness; check who is missing.

keyPoints: Numerical data are discrete or continuous; categorical data are nominal or ordinal.
Cleaning checks duplicates, formats and impossible values before any modelling.
Missing values can be deleted or imputed with mean, median or mode, and a missing flag can preserve information.
Min-max scaling maps x to (x − min) ÷ (max − min); standardisation maps x to (x − mean) ÷ standard deviation.
One-hot encoding makes a binary column per category; label encoding suits ordered categories.
Split data into training and test sets before modelling, fit preprocessing on training only, and check sampling bias.

en.title: Foundations of intelligent agents
en.short: Agents, environments, rationality, PEAS, environment properties and the five main agent architectures.

sections.heading: Agents and environments
sections.text: An agent is anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators. The environment is everything outside the agent. A percept is one reading; the percept sequence is the full history. An agent function maps percept sequences to actions, and an agent program implements that function on a physical or software agent. A rational agent chooses the action expected to maximise its performance measure, using its percept sequence and built-in knowledge. Rationality is not omniscience: it means doing the best expected, not knowing everything.

sections.heading: PEAS and rationality
sections.text: PEAS describes a task environment: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors. Example: Ada is a campus delivery robot at a Nigerian university. Performance: parcels delivered safely and on time. Environment: corridors, people, kerbs, weather. Actuators: wheels, brake, screen. Sensors: camera, distance sensor, bump sensor, battery monitor. PEAS forces you to state what success means before choosing methods.

sections.heading: Environment properties
sections.text: Environments vary. Fully observable means sensors see all relevant state; partially observable means some is hidden. Deterministic means the next state follows predictably from the current state and the action; stochastic means outcomes are uncertain. Episodic tasks are independent episodes; sequential tasks link decisions. Static environments do not change while the agent decides; dynamic ones do. Discrete environments have countable states and actions; continuous ones do not. Single-agent and multi-agent describe whether other agents affect outcomes. These properties decide which architecture is suitable.

sections.heading: Agent architectures
sections.text: A simple reflex agent uses condition-action rules on the current percept. It works well only when the environment is fully observable. A model-based reflex agent keeps internal state and a model of how the world changes, so it can act with hidden information. A goal-based agent considers future consequences and chooses actions that reach a goal. A utility-based agent compares outcomes using a utility function, which scores how good an outcome is, so it can handle trade-offs and uncertainty. A learning agent adds a learning element, critic and problem generator to improve its performance element over time. These designs frame later AI methods.

keyPoints: An agent perceives through sensors and acts through actuators.
A rational agent maximises expected performance using its percepts and knowledge, not by being omniscient.
PEAS stands for Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors.
Environment properties such as observability, determinism and dynamism guide architecture choice.
Simple reflex agents use current percepts; model-based agents keep internal state.
Goal-based agents plan towards goals, utility-based agents compare outcomes, and learning agents improve from feedback.

en.title: Uninformed search and state spaces
en.short: State-space formulation and BFS, DFS, uniform-cost, depth-limited and iterative deepening search.

sections.heading: State space
sections.text: Problem formulation turns a task into a state space: a set of states, an initial state, actions that move between states, a transition model giving each action’s result, a goal test, and a path cost. A solution is a path from the initial state to a goal; an optimal solution has the lowest path cost. The search tree unfolds paths from the initial state; repeated states make it differ from the state graph. Uninformed search uses only this formulation, with no estimate of distance to the goal.

sections.heading: Breadth and depth
sections.text:
Breadth-first search (BFS) expands the shallowest node first, using a queue. It is complete when the branching factor b is finite, and optimal when every step costs the same. Its time and space are O(b^d), where d is the depth of the shallowest goal; space is usually the limiting factor.

Depth-first search (DFS) expands the deepest node first, using a stack. It is not complete when a branch is infinite or loops occur, and it is not optimal. Its time is O(b^m), where m is the maximum depth, and its space is O(bm).

sections.heading: Costs and limits
sections.text:
Uniform-cost search (UCS) expands the node with the lowest path cost, using a priority queue. With finite branching and a positive minimum step cost ε, it is complete and optimal. Its time and space are O(b^(1+floor(C*/ε))), where C* is the optimal cost.

Depth-limited search (DLS) is DFS with a depth limit l. It is complete if l ≥ d, but not optimal. Time is O(b^l), space O(bl). Iterative deepening search (IDS) runs DLS with limits 0, 1, 2, ... until a goal is found. It is complete for finite b and optimal for equal step costs, with time O(b^d) and space O(bd).

Example: edges S-A 1, S-B 4, A-B 1, A-G 5, B-G 2. UCS expands S(0), A(1), B(2 via A), then G(4 via B), so the optimal cost is 4. BFS by edges would reach G at cost 6.

keyPoints: A search problem is defined by states, initial state, actions, transition model, goal test and path cost.
BFS is complete for finite branching and optimal for equal step costs, with time and space O(b^d).
DFS uses O(bm) space but is not complete on infinite branches and is not optimal.
UCS is complete and optimal with positive step costs; its time and space are O(b^(1+floor(C*/ε))).
DLS is complete when the limit reaches the goal depth, with time O(b^l) and space O(bl).
IDS is complete for finite branching and optimal for equal step costs, with time O(b^d) and space O(bd).

en.title: Informed search and heuristics
en.short: Best-first and A* search, heuristic functions, admissibility, consistency and heuristic quality.

sections.heading: Best-first and A*
sections.text:
Best-first search keeps a frontier of nodes ordered by an evaluation function and always expands the node with the smallest value. Greedy best-first uses f(n) = h(n), where h(n) is a heuristic estimate of the cost from n to a goal. It is fast but not optimal. A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the known cost from the start to n. With an admissible heuristic, A* is optimal on a tree; with a consistent heuristic, it is optimal on a graph without reopening closed nodes.

Example: S has edges S-A cost 1, S-B cost 4; A-G cost 5, B-G cost 1. Let h(S)=4, h(A)=3, h(B)=1, h(G)=0. A* starts with S (f=4), expands A (g=1, f=4), then B (g=4, f=5), then G via B (g=5, f=5). The optimal cost is 5.

sections.heading: Heuristic properties
sections.text: A heuristic is admissible if h(n) ≤ h*(n), the true cheapest cost from n to a goal, for every node. It never overestimates. A heuristic is consistent if h(n) ≤ c(n,n') + h(n') for every edge n to n', where c is the edge cost. Consistency implies admissibility. If h(goal)=0, consistency along a path gives h(n) ≤ true cost. Consistency also keeps A* from reopening nodes in graph search.

sections.heading: Quality and effort
sections.text: Better heuristics reduce the number of expanded nodes. A perfect heuristic expands only the solution path; h=0 makes A* uniform-cost search. Heuristic quality is often measured by the effective branching factor b*: N ≈ (b*)^d for depth d and N expansions. A heuristic h2 dominates h1 if h2(n) ≥ h1(n) for all n and both are admissible; h2 usually expands fewer nodes. Relaxed problems, such as ignoring a constraint, give admissible heuristics. Weighted A* uses f = g + w h with w > 1; it is faster but may return a suboptimal path.

keyPoints: Best-first search expands the frontier node with the smallest evaluation value.
Greedy best-first uses f(n) = h(n) and is not optimal.
A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) and is optimal with an admissible heuristic on a tree and a consistent heuristic on a graph.
Admissibility requires h(n) ≤ h*(n); consistency requires h(n) ≤ c(n,n') + h(n').
Consistency implies admissibility and prevents reopening nodes in graph search.
Better heuristics, such as dominating or relaxed-problem heuristics, reduce the number of expanded nodes.

en.title: Adversarial search and games
en.short: Minimax, alpha-beta pruning, expectiminimax, evaluation functions and game-tree search.

sections.heading: Game trees and minimax
sections.text:
Adversarial search plans against an opponent. In a two-player zero-sum game, one player’s gain is the other’s loss. A game tree has states as nodes, moves as edges and terminal utilities at leaves. Minimax backs values up: MAX picks the largest child value, MIN the smallest. Terminal nodes have utilities; other nodes take max or min over children.

Example: a MAX root has two MIN children. Left MIN sees leaves 3 and 5, so takes 3. Right MIN sees 2 and 8, so takes 2. MAX chooses max(3, 2) = 3.

sections.heading: Alpha-beta pruning
sections.text:
Alpha-beta pruning keeps two bounds. Alpha is the best value MAX can guarantee; beta is the best MIN can guarantee. Search stops below a node when alpha ≥ beta, because the opponent would never allow that line. With perfect ordering it examines about O(b^(d/2)) nodes instead of O(b^d), where b is branching factor and d depth. It returns the same value as minimax.

In the example, the left branch gives alpha = 3. The right MIN takes leaf 2, so beta = 2. Since 3 ≥ 2, leaf 8 is pruned.

sections.heading: Chance and expectiminimax
sections.text:
Expectiminimax adds chance nodes for dice, cards or random events. A chance node’s value is the weighted average of its children, using their probabilities. MAX still maximises and MIN still minimises.

Example: a chance node with probability 0.5 of 10 and 0.5 of 2 has value 0.5×10 + 0.5×2 = 6. Chance makes pruning less effective because averages can lie between bounds.

sections.heading: Evaluation and cutoffs
sections.text:
Full game trees are usually too large. Depth-limited search cuts off at a chosen depth and applies an evaluation function, a heuristic estimate of utility from MAX’s viewpoint. It often combines features such as material and mobility with weights. The same backup is used at the cutoff.

A bad cutoff causes the horizon effect, where a threat just beyond the search depth is missed. Iterative deepening and transposition tables help manage time and repeated states.

keyPoints: Minimax value: V(s) = utility(s) at a terminal, otherwise max over children for MAX and min over children for MIN.
Alpha-beta prunes a branch when alpha ≥ beta and returns the same value as minimax.
With perfect move ordering alpha-beta examines about O(b^(d/2)) nodes instead of O(b^d).
Expectiminimax gives a chance node the value Σ P(s') V(s'), the probability-weighted average of its children.
An evaluation function estimates utility at a depth cutoff and must be used consistently from MAX’s viewpoint.
Depth limits cause the horizon effect, where a threat just beyond the cutoff is missed.

en.title: Constraint satisfaction problems
en.short: CSP formulation, backtracking, forward checking, arc consistency and ordering heuristics.

sections.heading: Formulating a CSP
sections.text: A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) has variables, a domain of values for each variable, and constraints that limit which combinations are allowed. A solution assigns one value to every variable and satisfies every constraint. Constraints may be unary, binary or involve more variables. Example: four regions A, B, C, D must be coloured with colours {1,2,3}; adjacent pairs A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A must differ. There are 3^4 = 81 complete assignments before constraints are applied.

sections.heading: Backtracking search
sections.text: Backtracking search builds a solution one variable at a time. It picks an unassigned variable, tries a value consistent with the current partial assignment, and recurses. If no value works, it undoes the last choice and tries another. The search is complete: it finds a solution if one exists. Its worst-case cost is exponential in the number of variables, so pruning matters. For example, A=1, B=2, C=1, D=2 is valid.

sections.heading: Forward checking and propagation
sections.text: Forward checking is a form of constraint propagation. After assigning a variable, it removes from each unassigned neighbour’s domain every value that conflicts with the assignment. If a domain becomes empty, the search backtracks. Arc consistency is stronger: for every value of X, some value of Y must satisfy the binary constraint between X and Y. AC-3 repeatedly removes unsupported values using a queue of arcs. For X {1,2}, Y {1,2} and X<Y, arc consistency removes X=2 and Y=1, leaving X {1}, Y {2}. Arc consistency can still miss failures that need several variables together.

sections.heading: Ordering heuristics
sections.text: Variable ordering can change search size greatly. The minimum remaining values (MRV) heuristic chooses the variable with the fewest legal values, detecting dead ends early. The degree heuristic breaks ties by choosing the variable in the most constraints. Value ordering uses the least constraining value heuristic: try the value that rules out fewest values for neighbours. These heuristics do not change completeness, only speed.

keyPoints: A CSP has variables, domains and constraints; a solution assigns every variable and satisfies every constraint.
Backtracking search is complete but its worst case is exponential in the number of variables.
Forward checking removes conflicting values from neighbours and backtracks when a domain becomes empty.
Arc consistency requires every value of X to have a supporting value of Y; AC-3 enforces it.
The minimum remaining values heuristic chooses the variable with the fewest legal values, and the degree heuristic breaks ties.
The least constraining value heuristic tries the value that rules out fewest values for neighbours.

en.title: Knowledge representation and ontologies
en.short: Semantic networks, frames, description logic and ontologies, plus the cost of expressive inference.

sections.heading: Networks and frames
sections.text: A semantic network represents knowledge as a graph: nodes are concepts or individuals, and labelled edges are relations. A frame is a record-like structure with slots for properties and fillers for values. Both make inheritance easy: if every Vehicle has a wheelCount slot, a Car can inherit it. They are readable, but their meaning can be ambiguous, especially with defaults and exceptions. A default says what usually holds, not what must hold.

sections.heading: Description logic
sections.text: Description logic (DL) is a family of formal languages with concepts (classes), roles (relations) and individuals. It has a model-theoretic semantics, so a reasoner can answer questions precisely. Typical tasks are consistency (is the knowledge base contradictory?), subsumption (is one concept a subset of another?) and instance checking. For example, if Doctor ⊑ Person (every Doctor is a Person) and Doctor(DrOkafor) is asserted, a reasoner infers Person(DrOkafor). DL uses the open-world assumption: missing facts are unknown, not false.

sections.heading: Ontologies
sections.text: An ontology is an explicit, formal specification of a shared conceptualisation. In practice it is a set of classes, relations, individuals and axioms, often written in OWL (Web Ontology Language) and exchanged in RDF (Resource Description Framework). Ontologies support data integration and reuse: a clinic in Lagos and one in Nairobi can map their local terms to shared concepts. Ontology engineering needs domain experts and maintenance, so it is costly.

sections.heading: Expressive power trade-off
sections.text: The central trade-off is expressive power (how much you can say) against tractable inference (reasoning that stays computationally practical). More constructs, such as cardinalities, disjunction or inverse roles, let you say more but can make reasoning slower or undecidable. OWL 2 has profiles (EL, QL, RL) designed for different reasoning costs. Choose the weakest language that captures the needed distinctions, and test the reasoner on realistic data.

keyPoints: Semantic networks and frames are intuitive but can have ambiguous semantics.
Description logic gives formal semantics and decidable inference for many useful languages.
Ontologies are formal, shared specifications, often written in OWL.
Reasoning tasks include consistency, subsumption and instance checking.
The open-world assumption treats missing information as unknown, not false.
More expressive ontology languages usually make inference harder; choose the weakest adequate language.

en.title: Propositional logic and inference
en.short: Truth tables, resolution and DPLL for entailment, plus the limits of propositional logic.

sections.heading: Models and entailment
sections.text:
Propositional logic builds formulas from atoms such as P and Q, each of which is either true or false, using not, and, or, implies and iff. A model is one assignment of true or false to every atom. A knowledge base KB entails a sentence α when every model that makes KB true also makes α true.

Entailment can be tested another way: KB entails α exactly when KB together with not α has no model at all, that is, is unsatisfiable. So inference reduces to proving unsatisfiability.

sections.heading: Truth tables and resolution
sections.text:
A truth table lists all 2ⁿ models for n atoms, so the method is exact but exponential. Example: let KB be (P implies Q) and P, and ask whether Q follows. The only model making KB true has P true and Q true. In that row Q is true, so KB entails Q.

Resolution works on clauses, which are disjunctions of literals, in conjunctive normal form. From (A or B) and (not A or C) derive the resolvent (B or C). Adding resolvents until the empty clause appears proves the clauses unsatisfiable.

sections.heading: DPLL and its limits
sections.text:
DPLL is a complete backtracking SAT solver. It repeats unit propagation, where a clause whose other literals are all false forces its one unassigned literal to be true, and pure literal assignment, where a literal that appears only positively or only negatively in all clauses is set to satisfy them, then splits on an atom and recurses. Practical solvers add watched literals and clause learning. Satisfiability was the first problem proved NP-complete (Cook, 1971).

Propositional logic has real limits. It cannot state relations between objects, count, or say that all students pass, because it has no variables or quantifiers. Its formulas can also grow very large. These gaps motivate first-order logic.

keyPoints: KB entails α when every model of KB is a model of α.
KB entails α exactly when KB together with not α is unsatisfiable.
A truth table has 2ⁿ rows for n atoms, so it is exponential.
Resolution derives the empty clause exactly when the clauses are unsatisfiable.
DPLL combines unit propagation, pure literals and backtracking search.
Propositional logic cannot express relations or quantifiers, so first-order logic is needed.

en.title: First-order logic and inference
en.short: First-order syntax and semantics, quantifiers, unification, chaining and resolution, with a look at logic programming.

sections.heading: Syntax and semantics
sections.text:
First-order logic builds statements from terms and predicates. A term is a constant (Ada), a variable (x), or a function applied to terms (father(x)). An atom is a predicate applied to terms, such as Teaches(x, Ada); atoms joined by ¬, ∧, ∨ and → form formulas.

An interpretation supplies a domain and maps constants to objects, function symbols to functions, and predicates to sets of tuples. A formula is true when it holds under that assignment. KB ⊨ α means every model of KB is a model of α.

sections.heading: Quantifiers and unification
sections.text:
∀x P holds for every object; ∃x P for at least one. Order matters: ∀x∃y Loves(x,y) says everyone loves someone; ∃y∀x Loves(x,y) says one object is loved by all. ¬∀x P is equivalent to ∃x ¬P.

Unification finds a substitution making two atoms identical. Knows(John, x) and Knows(John, Mary) unify with {x/Mary}; Knows(John, x) and Knows(Bill, y) do not, since the constants differ. The most general unifier commits least, and an occurs check blocks {x/f(x)}.

sections.heading: Forward and backward chaining
sections.text: A Horn clause has at most one positive literal; a definite clause has exactly one, written head ← body. Forward chaining is data driven: from the facts, repeatedly fire rules whose premises match and add the conclusions, until nothing new appears. Backward chaining is goal driven: to prove a goal, find a rule whose head unifies with it and prove the premises as subgoals. Both are sound and complete for definite clauses.

sections.heading: Resolution and logic programming
sections.text:
Resolution proves KB ⊨ α by refutation: add ¬α, convert to clause form (Skolem functions remove ∃), and resolve complementary literals until the empty clause □ appears. Unification picks the literals; resolution is refutation-complete.

Logic programming applies this. A Prolog program is a set of definite clauses; a query runs backward chaining with unification and depth-first search. Given parent(ade, bola), parent(bola, chi) and grandparent(x,z) ← parent(x,y) ∧ parent(y,z), the query grandparent(ade, z) binds y = bola, then z = chi. Clause order changes what Prolog finds, so it is not a complete prover.

keyPoints: First-order logic adds terms, predicates and quantifiers to propositional logic, so it can describe objects and relations.
∀x P means P holds for all objects and ∃x P means it holds for at least one; ¬∀x P is equivalent to ∃x ¬P.
Unification finds the most general substitution that makes two atoms identical.
Forward chaining is data driven and backward chaining is goal driven; both are sound and complete for definite clauses.
Resolution proves KB ⊨ α by refuting KB ∧ ¬α using clause form, Skolemisation and unification, and is refutation-complete.
Prolog runs backward chaining with depth-first search, so clause order affects whether a query succeeds.

en.title: Classical planning
en.short: State-space planning, STRIPS operators, forward and backward search, partial-order plans and heuristics.

sections.heading: Planning as search
sections.text: Classical planning assumes a deterministic, fully observable, static world with one agent. A state is a set of facts held true, such as At(truck, Kano). An action changes one state into another. A plan is a sequence of actions from the initial state to a goal state. Planning can therefore be treated as state-space search: nodes are states, edges are actions, and a solution is a path. The search algorithms themselves belong to the search topics; here the concern is how states and actions are represented.

sections.heading: STRIPS operators
sections.text: STRIPS represents an action by an operator schema with parameters, preconditions, an add list and a delete list. Preconditions must hold before the action. The add list contains facts made true; the delete list contains facts made false. All other facts stay unchanged, which is the STRIPS assumption. For example, Drive(?from, ?to) may require At(truck, ?from) and Road(?from, ?to), add At(truck, ?to), and delete At(truck, ?from). Grounding replaces variables with objects.

sections.heading: Forward and backward
sections.text: Forward planning, or progression, starts at the initial state and applies applicable actions until a goal state is reached. Backward planning, or regression, starts from the goal and selects actions whose add list achieves a goal fact, replacing that fact with the action’s preconditions. It must also respect delete lists. Backward search can branch less, but both are complete for finite STRIPS problems.

sections.heading: Partial order and heuristics
sections.text: Partial-order planning builds a plan as steps plus ordering constraints and causal links. A causal link records that step A achieves condition c for step B. The planner adds steps only when needed, so it commits late. A threat is a step that could delete c; the planner adds an ordering constraint to remove it. Heuristics guide search: goal count, ignore-delete-lists relaxation, h_max and h_add, landmarks, and planning graphs. Ignoring delete lists makes planning easier but can mislead.

keyPoints: Classical planning searches from an initial state to a goal through deterministic actions.
STRIPS operators have preconditions, add lists and delete lists, and unchanged facts persist.
Forward planning progresses from the initial state; backward planning regresses from the goal.
Partial-order planning uses steps, ordering constraints and causal links, and resolves threats by ordering.
Planning heuristics estimate search distance, often by relaxing the problem, for example by ignoring delete lists.
Delete relaxation makes actions only add facts, so it is easier but can give misleading estimates.

en.title: Uncertainty and probabilistic reasoning
en.short: Probability for uncertainty, conditional independence, Bayes’ rule, naive Bayes and simple inference.

sections.heading: Probability as a language
sections.text: An agent rarely knows everything. Probability is a language for uncertainty: instead of true or false, a statement gets a number from 0 to 1. A random variable takes values with a probability distribution, and a joint distribution P(X, Y) covers every combination. Probabilities can be read as long-run frequencies or as degrees of belief.

sections.heading: Conditional independence
sections.text: Two variables X and Y are conditionally independent given Z when P(X, Y | Z) = P(X | Z) P(Y | Z). Once Z is known, X tells you nothing extra about Y. This matters because it lets a large joint distribution factor into small pieces, so we need far fewer numbers. For example, given a disease, two symptoms may be treated as independent though correlated overall.

sections.heading: Bayes’ rule
sections.text:
Bayes’ rule updates a belief when evidence arrives:
P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) ÷ P(E)
P(H) is the prior, P(E | H) the likelihood, and P(H | E) the posterior. P(E) normalises the result and is often found by summing P(E | h) P(h) over all hypotheses h. The rule follows from P(H | E) = P(H, E) ÷ P(E).

sections.heading: Naive Bayes and inference
sections.text:
A naive Bayes model predicts a class C from features X1 to Xn. It assumes the features are conditionally independent given C:
P(C | X1, …, Xn) ∝ P(C) Π P(Xi | C).
Inference means computing a posterior or marginal from a model. We compute unnormalised scores and divide by their sum.

Example: P(spam) = 0.3, P(ham) = 0.7. For the words free and meeting: P(free | spam) = 0.6, P(free | ham) = 0.1, P(meeting | spam) = 0.1, P(meeting | ham) = 0.5.
spam score = 0.3 × 0.6 × 0.1 = 0.018
ham score = 0.7 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.035
total = 0.053
P(spam | message) = 0.018 ÷ 0.053 ≈ 0.34
P(ham | message) = 0.035 ÷ 0.053 ≈ 0.66
So the message is ham.

keyPoints: Probability expresses uncertainty as a number from 0 to 1.
Conditional independence: P(X, Y | Z) = P(X | Z) P(Y | Z).
Bayes’ rule: P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) ÷ P(E).
Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class: P(C | X) ∝ P(C) Π P(Xi | C).
Inference computes a posterior or marginal, often by unnormalised scores divided by their sum.
Conditional independence reduces the number of probabilities a model needs.

en.title: Bayesian networks
en.short: Bayesian network structure, conditional probability tables, variable elimination and sampling.

sections.heading: Representation
sections.text: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph. Each node is a random variable; each edge points from a parent that directly influences a child. The graph encodes conditional independence: a node is independent of its non-descendants given its parents. The joint distribution factorises as P(X1,...,Xn) = ∏ P(Xi | parents(Xi)). This can be far smaller than a full joint table.

sections.heading: Conditional tables
sections.text:
Each node stores a conditional probability table (CPT). For a Boolean node with k Boolean parents the CPT has 2^k rows, one probability for each parent setting.

For example, P(Rain) = 0.2. P(Sprinkler | Rain) gives P(S=1 | R=1)=0.1 and P(S=1 | R=0)=0.5. P(Wet | Rain, Sprinkler) gives P(W=1 | R=1,S=1)=0.99, P(W=1 | R=1,S=0)=0.9, P(W=1 | R=0,S=1)=0.8, P(W=1 | R=0,S=0)=0.0.

sections.heading: Exact inference
sections.text:
Exact inference asks for a posterior, a probability updated after seeing evidence, such as P(R=1 | W=1). Variable elimination multiplies factors (tables over a few variables), sums out one variable at a time, and normalises. Eliminate S: f(R,W) = Σ_s P(S=s | R) P(W | R,S=s). Then multiply by P(R) and normalise.

For the CPTs above, P(W=1) = 0.0198 + 0.162 + 0.32 + 0 = 0.5018, and P(R=1,W=1)=0.1818, so P(R=1 | W=1)=0.1818 ÷ 0.5018 ≈ 0.362. The cost depends on the largest factor created, often measured by treewidth, roughly how tree-like the graph is.

sections.heading: Sampling
sections.text:
Approximate inference draws samples from the network. Direct sampling draws each variable in parent-before-child order from its CPT, then counts samples matching the query. Rejection sampling keeps only samples that agree with the evidence. Likelihood weighting fixes evidence variables to their observed values and weights each sample by the probability of those observed values given the sampled parents.

With enough samples the estimate approaches the true posterior, but the error falls slowly, roughly as 1 ÷ √N. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods such as Gibbs sampling are also used.

keyPoints: Joint distribution: P(X1,...,Xn) = ∏ P(Xi | parents(Xi)).
A CPT gives P(node | parent assignment); a Boolean node with k Boolean parents needs 2^k rows.
Variable elimination computes exact posteriors by multiplying factors and summing out variables.
Exact inference can be exponential in the largest factor or treewidth.
Sampling gives approximate posteriors; error falls roughly as 1 ÷ √N.
Likelihood weighting handles evidence by weighting samples instead of rejecting them.

en.title: Machine learning fundamentals
en.short: Supervised and unsupervised learning, overfitting, regularisation, cross-validation and evaluation metrics.

sections.heading: Learning types
sections.text: Supervised learning uses labelled examples, each input paired with a target. The model learns a mapping from input to output. A class target gives classification; a number target gives regression. Unsupervised learning uses inputs without labels and looks for structure, such as clusters.

sections.heading: Generalisation
sections.text: Training error is the error on data used to fit. Test error is the error on new, unseen data. A model that fits training data well but fails on test data has overfit: it learned noise. Underfitting is the opposite, with high error on both. Regularisation adds a penalty for large weights to the loss, for example λΣw², where λ controls strength. This trades training fit for better generalisation. Keep a final test set untouched.

sections.heading: Cross-validation
sections.text: Cross-validation estimates test error when data are limited. In k-fold cross-validation, split the data into k folds. Train on k − 1 folds and validate on the remaining fold. Repeat so each fold is validation once, then average the k errors. Use it to choose hyperparameters such as λ. Keep the final test set separate.

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics
sections.text: Classification metrics use a confusion matrix. Let TP, FP, FN and TN mean true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Accuracy is (TP + TN) ÷ total. Precision is TP ÷ (TP + FP), share of predicted positives that are correct. Recall is TP ÷ (TP + FN), share of real positives found. F1 = 2 × precision × recall ÷ (precision + recall). For regression, with actual y and predicted ŷ, MAE = (1/n)Σ|y − ŷ|, MSE = (1/n)Σ(y − ŷ)², RMSE = √MSE, and R² = 1 − SSres ÷ SStot (residual and total sums of squares). Example: 100 cases give TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 5, TN = 45. Accuracy = 85 ÷ 100 = 0.85. Precision = 40 ÷ 50 = 0.80. Recall = 40 ÷ 45 = 0.889. F1 = 80 ÷ 95 = 0.842.

keyPoints: Supervised learning uses labelled data; unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data.
Training error measures fit to seen data, while test error estimates performance on unseen data.
Overfitting gives low training error and high test error; regularisation adds a penalty such as λΣw² to reduce it.
In k-fold cross-validation, train on k − 1 folds, validate on the remaining fold, and average the k validation errors.
Classification metrics include accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ total, precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP), recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN) and F1 = 2 × precision × recall ÷ (precision + recall).
Regression metrics include MAE = (1/n)Σ|y − ŷ|, MSE = (1/n)Σ(y − ŷ)², RMSE = √MSE and R² = 1 − SSres ÷ SStot.

en.title: Neural networks and deep learning basics
en.short: Perceptrons, multilayer networks, backpropagation, activation functions, CNNs and RNNs.

sections.heading: The perceptron
sections.text:
A perceptron is the simplest artificial neuron: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the total through an activation function. With a step function it outputs 1 if Σwx + b > 0 and 0 otherwise. Training adjusts the weights from errors.

A single perceptron can only separate classes by a straight line or plane, so it cannot learn XOR.

sections.heading: Layers and activations
sections.text:
Stacking perceptrons in layers gives a multilayer network: an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Without a nonlinear activation function, stacked layers collapse into one linear map, so nonlinearity is essential.

Common choices: sigmoid, squashing to (0,1); tanh, to (−1,1); ReLU, max(0, z), cheap and fast to train; and softmax on the output layer for class probabilities.

Enough hidden units let a network approximate any continuous function, but that says nothing about learning from limited data.

sections.heading: Backpropagation
sections.text:
Training minimises a loss, such as mean squared error. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute the loss gradient for every weight, working backwards from the output. Gradient descent updates each weight: w ← w − η ∂L/∂w, with η the learning rate.

Example: x = 2, w = 0.5, b = 0.1, target y = 3, L = ½(y − ŷ)².
ŷ = 0.5 × 2 + 0.1 = 1.1
∂L/∂w = −(y − ŷ)x = −1.9 × 2 = −3.8
w ← 0.5 − 0.1 × (−3.8) = 0.88
New output 0.88 × 2 + 0.1 = 1.86, closer to 3.

sections.heading: Convolutional and recurrent
sections.text:
A convolutional network (CNN) slides small learned filters over an image, sharing the same weights across positions. This detects local patterns with far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer, and pooling shrinks the map.

A recurrent network (RNN) processes a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state that summarises the past. Plain RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies because gradients shrink or explode; gated variants such as LSTM and GRU address this.

keyPoints: A perceptron computes Σwx + b then applies an activation; alone it separates only linearly separable classes.
Hidden layers with nonlinear activations let a network fit curved boundaries; without them, depth adds nothing.
Backpropagation computes gradients by the chain rule, and gradient descent updates w ← w − η ∂L/∂w.
Sigmoid, tanh and ReLU are the standard hidden activations; softmax turns outputs into class probabilities.
CNNs share filter weights across space for images; RNNs share weights across time through a hidden state.
Vanishing and exploding gradients limit plain RNNs on long sequences; LSTM and GRU gates reduce the problem.

en.title: Natural language processing
en.short: Text normalisation, tokenisation, language models, tagging, parsing, embeddings and core NLP tasks.

sections.heading: From text to tokens
sections.text: Text normalisation puts raw text into a standard form: it may lowercase letters, remove punctuation or HTML, expand abbreviations, and correct encoding. Tokenisation splits text into tokens, usually words, subwords or characters. Word tokenisation is simple for spaced text but hard for languages without spaces and for contractions. Subword tokenisation, such as byte-pair encoding, splits rare words into frequent pieces and keeps the vocabulary small. A common pipeline is normalise, tokenise, then map tokens to integer IDs.

sections.heading: Language models
sections.text: A language model assigns a probability to a sequence of tokens. An n-gram model uses the previous n−1 tokens as context: P(w1...wm) = Π P(wi | wi−n+1...wi−1). In the sentence "the cat sat on the mat", "the" occurs twice, before "cat" and before "mat", so a bigram model gives P(cat | the) = 1/2 and P(mat | the) = 1/2. Unseen n-grams get zero probability, so smoothing adds small counts. Neural language models learn dense context representations and usually predict better.

sections.heading: Tagging and parsing
sections.text: Part-of-speech tagging labels each token with its grammatical class, such as noun, verb or determiner. A tagger may use rules, a hidden Markov model or a neural network. Parsing recovers structure: constituency parsing builds nested phrases, while dependency parsing links each word to a head word with a grammatical relation. Both tasks help downstream systems use syntax, for example to find the subject of a verb.

sections.heading: Embeddings and tasks
sections.text: Word embeddings map words to dense vectors so that similar words lie close together. Word2vec learns vectors by predicting a word from its neighbours, while GloVe learns from global co-occurrence counts; contextual models such as BERT produce different vectors for a word in different sentences. Standard NLP tasks include text classification, such as spam detection, and machine translation, which maps a source sentence to a target sentence. Modern translation systems use sequence-to-sequence neural networks with attention. Evaluation uses task-specific measures, such as accuracy for classification and BLEU for translation, which scores n-gram overlap with reference translations.

keyPoints: Text normalisation standardises raw text before tokenisation splits it into words or subwords.
An n-gram language model estimates P(w1...wm) = Π P(wi | wi−n+1...wi−1).
Part-of-speech tagging labels tokens, and parsing recovers phrase or dependency structure.
Word embeddings represent words as dense vectors that capture similarity.
Text classification and machine translation are standard NLP tasks.
BLEU is a common evaluation measure for machine translation, but it is not the same as human judgement.

en.title: Computer vision
en.short: Image formation, filtering, features, convolutional networks, object detection and segmentation.

sections.heading: Images and formation
sections.text: An image is a grid of pixels, each holding intensity or colour values. A grey image has one channel; a colour image usually has red, green and blue channels. The pinhole camera model describes formation: a 3D point projects to image coordinates through a camera centre and focal length. Perspective makes distant objects smaller. Images are represented as arrays, so vision tasks become operations on numbers.

sections.heading: Filtering
sections.text: Filtering changes an image by combining each pixel with its neighbours. Convolution slides a small kernel over the image and sums products. An averaging kernel blurs and reduces noise; a kernel with positive and negative weights, such as the Laplacian, responds to edges. Example: patch rows 1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9 with kernel rows 0 1 0; 1 -4 1; 0 1 0 gives 0×1+1×2+0×3+1×4−4×5+1×6+0×7+1×8+0×9 = 0. The zero response fits a smooth gradient. Filters are linear; pooling is a later non-linear downsampling step.

sections.heading: Features and CNNs
sections.text: Feature extraction finds useful local patterns: edges, corners, blobs (spot-like regions) and texture. Classical detectors use gradients and scale-space, for example SIFT for scale-invariant keypoints. A convolutional network learns filters instead of hand-designing them. Convolution layers share weights across positions, so they detect a pattern anywhere. Pooling reduces resolution. Stacked layers build from edges to parts to objects; a classifier head gives class scores.

sections.heading: Detection and segmentation
sections.text: Object detection finds objects and their bounding boxes. A detector scores candidate boxes and keeps those above a threshold, then non-maximum suppression removes overlapping duplicates. Intersection over union (IoU) measures box overlap. Segmentation labels pixels: semantic segmentation gives a class per pixel, instance segmentation separates individual objects. Fully convolutional networks and U-Net style models are common. Masks are evaluated with IoU or pixel accuracy.

keyPoints: An image is an array of pixel values, and the pinhole model explains how 3D points project to 2D image coordinates.
Convolution computes a weighted sum of a local patch and a kernel, so kernels can blur or detect edges.
Convolutional layers learn shared filters and pooling reduces spatial resolution.
Object detectors predict bounding boxes and use IoU and non-maximum suppression to clean up detections.
Semantic segmentation labels every pixel, while instance segmentation separates individual objects.
For a filter, output(x,y) = ΣΣ I(x+i,y+j)K(i,j); for boxes, IoU = overlap area ÷ union area.

en.title: Robotics and embodied AI
en.short: Robot perception, localisation, mapping, planning and control through the sense-plan-act loop.

sections.heading: Sense, plan, act
sections.text: An embodied AI system has a body, sensors and actuators. It runs a loop: sense the world, update a belief, plan an action, act, then sense again. A belief is a probability distribution over possible states, such as pose (position and orientation). The loop matters because actions change the world and sensors are noisy.

sections.heading: Perception and localisation
sections.text:
Perception turns raw sensor data into useful estimates: obstacles, landmarks, or the robot’s pose. Localisation is estimating pose on a known map. Because sensors are noisy, probabilistic robotics represents belief as a probability distribution and updates it with Bayes’ rule. A motion model predicts the belief after movement; a measurement model corrects it after a sensor reading.

Example: prior belief 0.6 at A and 0.4 at B. A door sensor is true with probability 0.9 at A and 0.2 at B. After seeing the door:
P(A|door) = (0.9 × 0.6) ÷ (0.9 × 0.6 + 0.2 × 0.4) = 0.54 ÷ 0.62 ≈ 0.871.
P(B|door) ≈ 0.129.

sections.heading: Mapping and planning
sections.text: Mapping builds a map from sensor data. An occupancy grid stores the probability that each cell is occupied. SLAM solves localisation and mapping together when the map is unknown. Path planning finds a route from start to goal that avoids obstacles. It may search a graph of free space or sample random poses; the plan must respect the robot’s shape and motion limits. The map may be 2D or 3D.

sections.heading: Control and uncertainty
sections.text: Control turns a plan into actuator commands. Feedback control compares the measured state with the desired state and corrects the error; PID control uses proportional, integral and derivative terms. Good robot systems plan under uncertainty and re-plan when beliefs change. Embodied AI adds learning; the sense-plan-act loop and probabilistic belief are the classical core, and many modern systems build on them.

keyPoints: The sense-plan-act loop links perception, planning, action and renewed sensing.
A belief is a probability distribution over possible robot states, such as pose.
Bayes’ rule updates belief: P(x|z) ∝ P(z|x)P(x), using motion and measurement models.
Localisation estimates pose on a known map; SLAM estimates pose and map together.
Path planning finds a collision-free route, and feedback control turns it into actuator commands.
PID control uses u = Kp e + Ki Σ e Δt + Kd Δe ÷ Δt, where e is the error.

en.title: Reinforcement learning
en.short: Markov decision processes, value and policy iteration, TD learning, Q-learning and exploration.

sections.heading: Markov decision processes
sections.text:
An MDP models an agent that sees state s, takes action a, receives reward r and moves to s′. It is defined by states S, actions A, transition probabilities P(s′|s,a), rewards R and a discount factor γ between 0 and 1. The Markov property says the next state and reward depend only on s and a, not on earlier history. A policy π maps each state to an action.

The return is G = r₀ + γr₁ + γ²r₂ + …, and Vπ(s) is its expected value from s. γ near 1 values long-term reward; γ near 0 is short-sighted.

sections.heading: Value and policy iteration
sections.text:
Value iteration applies V(s) := max over a of Σ P(s′|s,a)[R + γV(s′)] repeatedly until V stops changing much. Policy iteration alternates policy evaluation, which computes Vπ for the current policy, with policy improvement, which sets π(s) to a greedy action. Both converge for finite MDPs.

Example: one state, action A gives reward 1 and stays, action B gives 0, γ = 0.5. From V = 0, value iteration gives 1, then 1.5, then 1.75, tending to 1 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 2.

sections.heading: Temporal-difference learning
sections.text: TD learning learns values from experience without a model of P. TD(0) updates after each step: V(s) := V(s) + α[r + γV(s′) − V(s)], where α is the learning rate and the bracket is the TD error. It bootstraps: it updates a guess using another guess. TD(λ) blends this with Monte Carlo returns, which wait for the episode to end.

sections.heading: Q-learning and exploration
sections.text:
Q-learning learns action values without a model: Q(s,a) := Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max over a′ of Q(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)]. It is off-policy: it learns the greedy policy while behaving differently.

The exploration-exploitation trade-off is the choice between trying new actions to gain information and using the best known action to gain reward. ε-greedy picks a random action with probability ε and the greedy action otherwise; decaying ε over time is common.

keyPoints: An MDP is defined by (S, A, P, R, γ) and satisfies the Markov property.
Value iteration uses V(s) := max_a Σ P(s′|s,a)[R + γV(s′)]; policy iteration alternates evaluation and improvement.
TD(0) update: V(s) := V(s) + α[r + γV(s′) − V(s)].
Q-learning update: Q(s,a) := Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max_a′ Q(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)].
ε-greedy explores with probability ε and exploits otherwise.
The discount factor γ sets how much future reward counts.

en.title: AI ethics and governance
en.short: Bias, fairness, privacy, accountability, transparency, safety, labour and environmental effects, and AI regulation.

sections.heading: Bias and fairness
sections.text: Bias means systematic error that disadvantages a group. It enters through data, labels, features and deployment. Fairness is not one thing. Statistical parity asks for similar selection rates across groups. Equal opportunity asks for similar true positive rates among people who truly qualify. A hiring model trained on past hires that favoured men may reject qualified women. Suppose it selects 60% of men and 30% of women with similar qualifications; that gap is evidence of disparate impact, where an apparently neutral practice harms a protected group, though metrics can conflict. Fairness depends on context.

sections.heading: Privacy and accountability
sections.text: Privacy concerns personal data. Data minimisation collects what is needed; consent and purpose limitation restrict use; anonymisation removes identifiers, though re-identification is possible; differential privacy adds calibrated noise so outputs reveal little about any one person. Accountability means a named person or organisation can answer for an AI system: documented roles, audits, logs, complaint routes and redress. It cannot be delegated to the model.

sections.heading: Transparency and safety
sections.text: Transparency means disclosing that AI is used, what data it uses and its limits. Explainability helps users contest decisions, but a trade-off with accuracy is not automatic. Safety means testing for harmful failures before release, monitoring after release, and keeping human oversight for high-stakes decisions. A medical triage tool, for example, needs validation on local patients, a fallback when it fails, and a clinician able to override it.

sections.heading: Regulation and codes
sections.text: Approaches differ. The EU AI Act is risk-based: some uses are banned, high-risk systems face duties, and limited-risk uses need disclosure. GDPR governs personal data in the EU. The US has sectoral rules and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, a voluntary guide. The OECD AI Principles and UNESCO Recommendation are international soft law, meaning non-binding guidance. Professional codes such as the ACM Code of Ethics and the IEEE Code of Ethics set duties of competence, honesty and public welfare. Labour effects include job change and hidden data work such as labelling; environmental effects include energy, water and carbon from training and use. Check current law for your country.

keyPoints: Bias is systematic error; fairness metrics such as statistical parity and equal opportunity can conflict.
Privacy tools include data minimisation, consent, anonymisation and differential privacy.
Accountability requires named roles, audits, logs and redress, not just a model.
Transparency and explainability help people contest decisions, but they have limits.
Safety needs pre-release testing, monitoring and human oversight for high-stakes uses.
Regulation ranges from risk-based law to sectoral rules, voluntary frameworks and professional codes.

en.title: Advanced machine learning
en.short: Kernels, SVMs, ensembles, regularisation, model selection and probabilistic supervised learning.

sections.heading: Kernels and SVMs
sections.text:
A kernel k(x, z) returns an inner product in a feature space without building it: k(x, z) = φ(x)·φ(z). A valid kernel has a positive semi-definite Gram matrix. The kernel trick swaps inner products for k, so a linear method becomes nonlinear. Common kernels are polynomial (x·z + c)^d and RBF exp(−γ||x − z||²).

A support vector machine (SVM) maximises the margin 2 ÷ ||w|| by minimising ||w||² subject to y_i(w·x_i + b) ≥ 1. The soft margin adds slack variables and a cost C, giving hinge loss. Only support vectors lie on or inside the margin, and they alone set the boundary.

Example: k = (x·z + 1)², x = (1, 2), z = (3, 0). x·z = 1×3 + 2×0 = 3, so k = (3 + 1)² = 16.

sections.heading: Ensembles
sections.text: Bagging trains models on bootstrap samples and combines their predictions, which cuts variance; random forests also use random feature subsets to decorrelate the trees. Boosting fits weak learners in sequence, each one focusing on earlier errors, which cuts bias. AdaBoost and gradient boosting are common forms. Stacking learns a combiner over base models. Ensembles often beat a single model but cost more to train and are harder to explain.

sections.heading: Regularisation and model selection
sections.text: Regularisation adds a penalty on the weights to the loss. Ridge adds λ||w||², shrinking weights smoothly. Lasso adds λ||w||₁, which can set weights to zero and so select features. The strength λ is chosen by cross-validation: split the data into k folds, train on k − 1, test on the rest, and average the scores. Nested cross-validation keeps tuning separate from final evaluation. Test data must never be used for tuning.

sections.heading: Probabilistic approaches
sections.text: Probabilistic supervised learning models p(y | x), not just a label. Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ rule and assumes features are conditionally independent given the class; it is fast and works well on text. Logistic regression models the log-odds as a linear function, w·x + b, and is trained by maximising likelihood, equivalently minimising cross-entropy. Gaussian process regression puts a prior over functions and returns a predictive mean and variance.

keyPoints: A kernel k(x, z) equals φ(x)·φ(z), so linear methods become nonlinear without explicit features.
An SVM minimises ||w||² subject to y_i(w·x_i + b) ≥ 1, and the margin is 2 ÷ ||w||.
Bagging reduces variance; boosting reduces bias.
Ridge penalises λ||w||²; lasso penalises λ||w||₁ and can set weights to zero.
k-fold cross-validation estimates generalisation, and test data stay untouched.
Naive Bayes assumes conditional independence; logistic regression models log-odds as w·x + b.

en.title: Deep learning architectures
en.short: Training deep networks, regularisation, batch normalisation, CNNs, RNNs, attention and transformers.

sections.heading: Training and optimisation
sections.text: Deep networks are trained by minimising a loss function with gradient descent. The gradient points uphill, so parameters move against it. Stochastic gradient descent uses mini-batches, small random subsets of the training data, making steps noisy but cheap. Momentum accumulates past gradients to smooth the path.
