Adaptive methods such as Adam scale each coordinate using running estimates of gradient and squared gradient. The learning rate is critical: too large diverges, too small is slow. Backpropagation computes gradients by the chain rule.

sections.heading: Regularisation and normalisation
sections.text:
Regularisation limits overfitting. Weight decay penalises large weights. Dropout randomly removes units during training, forcing redundancy. Early stopping ends training when validation loss stops improving. Data augmentation creates input variants. Batch normalisation standardises each layer input over a mini-batch, then applies learned scale and shift. It often speeds optimisation and permits larger learning rates, though not essential everywhere.

Example: activations 1, 3, 5, 7. Mean = (1+3+5+7) ÷ 4 = 4. Variance = ((1−4)²+(3−4)²+(5−4)²+(7−4)²) ÷ 4 = 5. Standard deviation = √5 ≈ 2.236. Normalised values are (x−4) ÷ 2.236: −1.34, −0.45, 0.45, 1.34.

sections.heading: Convolution and recurrence
sections.text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) apply learned filters over local patches. Weight sharing lets one filter detect the same pattern anywhere, reducing parameters and giving translation equivariance. Pooling or strided convolution reduces spatial size. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) process sequences by carrying a hidden state from step to step. Plain RNNs suffer vanishing gradients over long spans. Long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) cells use gates to control what is kept or forgotten.

sections.heading: Attention and transformers
sections.text: Attention computes a weighted sum of values. A query is compared with keys to produce weights, usually by scaled dot-product softmax. This lets a model focus on relevant positions without recurrence. Transformers stack self-attention and feed-forward layers with residual connections and layer normalisation. Multi-head attention runs several attention maps in parallel. Positional encodings supply order information because self-attention alone ignores token order. Transformers train in parallel over positions, which made them dominant in language.

keyPoints: Gradient descent updates parameters against the gradient; Adam adapts per-coordinate steps.
Regularisation methods include weight decay, dropout, early stopping and data augmentation.
Batch normalisation computes xhat = (x − μ) ÷ √(σ² + ε), then y = γxhat + β.
CNNs share filter weights across positions; RNNs carry a hidden state and LSTM or GRU gates control memory.
Scaled dot-product attention weights values by softmax(QK^T ÷ √d).
Transformers stack self-attention and feed-forward layers and need positional encodings for order.

en.title: Probabilistic graphical models
en.short: Hidden Markov models, conditional random fields, variational inference, MCMC and causal graphs.

sections.heading: Hidden Markov models
sections.text:
A hidden Markov model (HMM) describes a sequence of hidden states that form a Markov chain, where each state emits an observed symbol. Its parameters are the initial state distribution, the transition probabilities and the emission probabilities.

Three tasks recur. Filtering uses the forward algorithm; smoothing uses forward-backward. The most likely state path comes from the Viterbi algorithm. Learning uses Baum-Welch, a form of expectation-maximisation.

Example: states Rain and Sun. P(R|R) = 0.7, P(S|R) = 0.3, P(R|S) = 0.4, P(S|S) = 0.6. Emissions: Rain gives umbrella 0.9, Sun gives umbrella 0.2. Start P(R) = 0.5. Observed: umbrella, umbrella.
Day 1: R = 0.5 × 0.9 = 0.45; S = 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.10; total 0.55.
Day 2: R = (0.45 × 0.7 + 0.10 × 0.4) × 0.9 = 0.355 × 0.9 = 0.3195; S = (0.45 × 0.3 + 0.10 × 0.6) × 0.2 = 0.195 × 0.2 = 0.039.
Total probability of the two observations is 0.3195 + 0.039 = 0.3585.

sections.heading: Conditional random fields
sections.text: A conditional random field (CRF) models the conditional probability of a label sequence given an observation sequence directly, as a log-linear function of clique potentials, normalised over all label sequences. It is discriminative: it never models the observations, so it can use overlapping, dependent features, unlike an HMM. Training maximises conditional likelihood, which is convex for a linear-chain CRF. Inference again uses forward-backward or Viterbi.

sections.heading: Approximate inference
sections.text:
Exact inference is intractable in large or dense graphs, so two families of approximation are used.

Variational inference picks a tractable family q and maximises the evidence lower bound, ELBO = E_q[log p(x, z)] − E_q[log q(z)], which equals log p(x) minus KL(q || p(z|x)). It is fast and gives a bound, but it is biased.

Markov chain Monte Carlo builds a chain whose stationary distribution is the target. Metropolis-Hastings accepts a proposal z' with probability min(1, [p(z') q(z|z')] ÷ [p(z) q(z'|z)]). Gibbs sampling is a special case. It is asymptotically exact but slower.

sections.heading: Causal graphical models
sections.text: The arrows in a Bayesian network need not mean causation. A causal graph adds the assumption that each arrow is a direct causal effect. The do-operator defines P(Y | do(X = x)): delete the arrows into X, fix X = x, and compute in the mutilated graph. The backdoor criterion tells you which variables to adjust for, namely a set that blocks every non-causal path between X and Y. Adjusting for a collider instead of a confounder introduces bias: a confounder is a common cause of X and Y, while a collider is a common effect of two other variables.

keyPoints: An HMM is defined by initial, transition and emission probabilities.
Forward-backward gives sequence likelihood; Viterbi gives the best state path.
A CRF models P(labels | observations) directly and avoids the HMM emission independence assumption.
Variational inference maximises the ELBO = E_q[log p(x, z)] − E_q[log q(z)].
Metropolis-Hastings accepts a proposal with probability min(1, [p(z') q(z|z')] ÷ [p(z) q(z'|z)]).
P(Y | do(X = x)) is computed by deleting arrows into X and fixing X = x.

en.title: Research methods in AI
en.short: Literature review, reproducible experiments, baselines, statistical evaluation, ethics and scientific writing.

sections.heading: Literature and design
sections.text: A literature review is a systematic search and synthesis, not a list of papers. Define a question, choose databases and search terms, set inclusion criteria, then group findings and state the gap your work fills. The design follows from that gap: state a testable hypothesis or research question, the data, the methods and the evaluation plan before you run experiments. Keep a lab notebook or version-controlled log.

sections.heading: Reproducible experiments
sections.text: Reproducibility means another researcher can obtain the same results from your code, data and description. Record random seeds, library versions, hardware, data splits and preprocessing. Release code and data where licences and privacy allow. A baseline is a reference method that a new method must beat; use simple baselines and strong published ones. An ablation study removes one component to show its effect.

sections.heading: Statistical evaluation
sections.text: One run is not evidence. Run several seeds or folds, report mean and spread, and use confidence intervals (ranges of plausible values). A significance test, such as a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test on matched splits, estimates whether a difference is likely due to chance; check its assumptions and report effect size (the size of the difference). Example: five seed accuracies 0.81, 0.83, 0.80, 0.82, 0.84 give mean 0.82 and sample standard deviation 0.016. Do not report only the best score.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Ethical approval is needed before collecting human data, personal data or sensitive material. Rules differ by institution and country; consult your ethics committee or institutional review board and the relevant data protection law. Scientific writing states the claim, method, results and limitations, gives enough detail to repeat the work, and avoids overclaiming. Cite data, code and prior work; report negative results honestly.

keyPoints: A literature review defines a question, searches systematically and states the gap the dissertation fills.
Reproducibility requires code, data, seeds, library versions and environment details; baselines are reference methods that a new method must beat.
One run is not evidence: report mean and spread over several seeds or folds, with confidence intervals and effect size.
Sample standard deviation is s = √(Σ(x − m)² ÷ (n − 1)), where m is the mean; for 0.81, 0.83, 0.80, 0.82, 0.84, m = 0.82 and s = 0.016.
Get ethical approval before collecting human or personal data; rules differ by institution and country.
Scientific writing states claim, method, results and limitations, and gives enough detail to repeat the work.
